cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a single anonymous report that a two-year-old was seen naked and unsupervised in her own driveway did not describe neglect under N.C.G.S. § 7B-101 and therefore never triggered the mandatory investigation power of § 7B-302, so the § 7B-303 non-interference order against the parents had to be reversed.
cases.quote: a single report of a naked, unsupervised two-year-old in the driveway of her home does not trigger the investigative requirements of N.C.G.S. § 7B-302

relevance.INP-01: Stumbo fixes the threshold a report must clear before the § 7B-301 reporting chain converts into a compulsory § 7B-302 investigation.
relevance.INP-02: It holds that a third-party report must actually allege facts amounting to abuse, neglect, or dependency before DSS acquires its statutory investigative powers.
relevance.INP-05: It confirms DSS may make voluntary inquiry and offer help on a low-level report without invoking the coercive Chapter 7B apparatus.
relevance.INP-06: The case arose from an anonymous hotline call and is the controlling NC authority on what an anonymous tip must contain.
relevance.INP-07: Any reporter's information, including from clinicians, must describe conduct meeting the statutory definitions before mandatory investigation attaches.
relevance.INP-08: School and other institutional reports are likewise measured against the § 7B-101 definitions before DSS gains § 7B-302 authority.
relevance.INP-10: Stumbo is the leading NC case on escalating a screened report to a mandated investigation and on the screening step that precedes it.
relevance.DEC-01: The Court expressly approved screening out reports that do not meet the statutory definitions of abuse, neglect, or dependency.
relevance.DEC-02: It marks the line between permissible informal inquiry and a mandated investigative assessment carrying compulsory process.
relevance.DEC-06: It endorses a non-coercive, service-oriented response to low-risk reports without invoking Chapter 7B petitions.
relevance.ACT-01: The Court noted that a phone call to the parents, not compulsory process, was the proportionate response on these facts.
relevance.ACT-06: It limits state intrusion into the family in response to an isolated supervision lapse not amounting to statutory neglect.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the statutory presumption of good faith for persons reporting suspected child abuse or neglect shifts to the plaintiff the burden of producing factual (not speculative) evidence of bad faith or malice, and that summary judgment for the reporter is proper absent such a forecast.
cases.quote: Evidence offered to meet or rebut the presumption of good faith must be sufficient by virtue of its reasonableness, not by mere supposition.

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling NC authority on the immunity and good-faith presumption that protect anyone who reports under N.C.G.S. § 7B-301.
relevance.INP-02: It sets the evidentiary burden a subject of a voluntary third-party report must meet to sue the reporter.
relevance.INP-06: It explains why anonymous and confidential hotline reporting is protected: good faith is presumed until factually rebutted.
relevance.INP-07: Health-care reporters enjoy the same presumption of good faith and statutory immunity described here.
relevance.INP-08: School personnel reporting suspected maltreatment are covered by the same immunity and presumption.
relevance.DEC-06: Because reporters are shielded, agencies can triage reports into non-court responses without fear of collateral defamation litigation driving decisions.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that verification of a juvenile petition under N.C.G.S. § 7B-403(a) is a jurisdictional prerequisite, so an unverified petition leaves the district court without subject matter jurisdiction and every order entered in the case is void ab initio.
cases.quote: the district court could not exercise subject matter jurisdiction here in the absence of the verification

relevance.INP-02: The Court recognized that a Chapter 7B action may begin from an anonymous or third-party report but stressed the statutory safeguards that must then be observed.
relevance.INP-04: Judicially triggered juvenile proceedings still require a properly verified DSS petition to confer jurisdiction.
relevance.INP-06: The opinion expressly acknowledges that anonymous reports may launch a case, which is why verification is treated as a vital safeguard.
relevance.DEC-05: Verification of the petition is the jurisdictional gateway to opening a dependency case in North Carolina.
relevance.OUT-05: An unverified petition requires dismissal because the court never acquired power to act.
relevance.FAIL-01: Lack of verification is a jurisdictional defect that may be raised at any time and voids the agency-obtained orders.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Juvenile Code does not confine the filing of an abuse, neglect, or dependency petition to the director of the county department of social services where the juvenile resides or is found, so a petition filed by another county director does not defeat subject matter jurisdiction.
cases.quote: the statute does not identify which county director of social services must file the petition

relevance.INP-04: It clarifies which agency may act on a referral and open a juvenile case, a recurring question when courts refer cases across county lines.
relevance.DEC-05: It defines who has standing to file the petition that opens a dependency case in North Carolina.
relevance.OUT-04: The opinion restates that once properly obtained, juvenile-court jurisdiction continues until terminated by order or until the juvenile turns eighteen or is emancipated.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court upheld the statutory neglect ground for termination and held that neglect turns on the circumstances and conditions surrounding the child rather than on parental fault, reversing the Court of Appeals' narrower construction.
cases.quote: In determining whether a child is neglected, the determinative factors are the circumstances and conditions surrounding the child, not the fault or culpability of the parent.

relevance.DEC-03: Montgomery supplies the substantive definition of neglect that an agency must satisfy to reach a founded finding.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the leading NC authority on the neglect ground for termination and on the two-stage adjudication/disposition structure.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that evidence of neglect predating loss of custody, including a prior adjudication, is admissible in a termination proceeding, but the trial court must make an independent present-day determination that weighs changed conditions against the history of neglect and the probability that neglect would recur.
cases.quote: The trial court must also consider any evidence of changed conditions in light of the evidence of prior neglect and the probability of a repetition of neglect.

relevance.ACT-02: Progress under a court-ordered service plan is the 'changed conditions' evidence the court must weigh before terminating on neglect.
relevance.OUT-01: Ballard is the authority a parent invokes to show corrected conditions supporting reunification rather than termination.
relevance.OUT-02: It bars treating a prior neglect adjudication as conclusive and requires a current finding of likely repetition.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed a termination order, holding that the trial court's findings did not support the conclusions of neglect or willful abandonment because the evidence failed to show a willful determination to forego all parental duties.
cases.quote: At the adjudication stage, the party petitioning for the termination must show by clear, cogent, and convincing evidence that grounds authorizing the termination of parental rights exist.

relevance.OUT-02: Young states the burden and two-stage structure governing every NC termination and shows that findings must actually support each ground.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the petitioner cannot meet the clear, cogent, and convincing standard, the petition fails and the case must be dismissed or reversed.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a parent's failure to comply with a court-approved case plan supports termination under N.C.G.S. § 7B-1111(a)(2) so long as the case plan provision addresses an issue that directly or indirectly contributed to the child's removal, and it reversed the Court of Appeals' contrary, narrower reading.
cases.quote: parental compliance with a judicially adopted case plan is relevant in determining whether grounds for termination exist

relevance.ACT-01: It marks the point at which voluntary cooperation becomes a judicially adopted plan whose terms carry termination consequences.
relevance.ACT-02: B.O.A. is the controlling NC authority on the permissible scope of court-ordered case plan requirements and their nexus to the conditions of removal.
relevance.OUT-01: Reasonable progress on nexus-related case plan components is what supports a return home rather than termination.
relevance.OUT-02: It governs the § 7B-1111(a)(2) 'reasonable progress' ground for termination.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a natural parent's paramount constitutional right to custody may be displaced in favor of a third party only on clear and convincing evidence of unfitness, neglect, or conduct inconsistent with the parent's protected status, and never merely because a different placement would be better for the child.
cases.quote: The Due Process Clause ensures that the government cannot unconstitutionally infringe upon a parent's paramount right to custody solely to obtain a better result for the child.

relevance.DEC-04: An emergency removal decision cannot rest on a judgment that another home would simply be better for the child.
relevance.ACT-03: Placement of a child outside the parental home requires clear and convincing proof displacing the parent's constitutional status.
relevance.ACT-04: Awarding custody to relatives or other third parties is constitutionally constrained by the same clear and convincing standard.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective orders that restrict a parent's contact must be grounded in more than a comparative best-interests judgment.
relevance.ACT-06: State intervention in the care of a child cannot override parental decision-making solely to obtain a better outcome.
relevance.FAIL-02: Removals not supported by clear and convincing evidence of unfitness or conduct inconsistent with parental status violate due process.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a trial court's finding that a parent is fit does not preclude a separate conclusion, supported by clear and convincing evidence, that the parent acted inconsistently with his constitutionally protected status, permitting custody to be shared with or given to third parties.
cases.quote: a determination that a natural parent has acted in a way inconsistent with his constitutionally protected status must be supported by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.ACT-03: It identifies the two distinct routes (unfitness, or conduct inconsistent with protected status) by which a parent may lose custody to the state or another caregiver.
relevance.ACT-04: It is the authority applied when kin or other third parties seek custody over a parent's objection.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held, in an appeal from a North Carolina termination order, that due process does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding; the trial court must decide case by case under the Eldridge factors, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: Lassiter is the federal constitutional floor for a parent's right to counsel in termination proceedings and arose out of a Durham County, North Carolina case.
relevance.FAIL-01: It supplies the federal standard against which a claimed denial of counsel or of a fair termination hearing is reviewed on appeal.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that before a State may permanently terminate parental rights, the Due Process Clause requires proof of its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence, striking down a preponderance standard.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: Santosky establishes that the more serious the state's intrusion on the parent-child relationship, the higher the constitutionally required standard of proof supporting the state's findings.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the federal constitutional source of North Carolina's clear, cogent, and convincing standard at the termination adjudication stage.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the 'reasonable efforts' requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act creates no federal right enforceable by children or parents through § 1983 or an implied right of action; enforcement lies with the Secretary through the state-plan approval process.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.INP-09: Suter explains why federal oversight of state child-welfare performance runs through administrative plan review rather than private litigation.
relevance.OUT-04: Title IV-E requirements governing foster care and transition services are enforced federally, not by suits brought by youth in care.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the controlling authority on the consequences and remedies for a state's failure to meet Title IV-E requirements.
relevance.PMC-01: It locates CFSR-style compliance monitoring in HHS's administrative apparatus rather than in private enforcement actions.
relevance.PMC-02: Federal financial oversight of child-welfare funds operates through the Secretary's plan-approval and audit powers, not private suits.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review and similar CAPTA structures are advisory oversight mechanisms, not privately enforceable entitlements.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability layer built on federal child-welfare statutes must account for the absence of a private right of action.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a state agency's failure to protect a child from violence by his father, even after repeated reports of abuse, did not deprive the child of liberty without due process because the Constitution imposes no general affirmative duty on the State to protect against private violence.
cases.quote: a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

relevance.OUT-06: DeShaney is the starting point for any claim arising from a child's death or serious injury after CPS involvement but while in parental custody.
relevance.FAIL-03: It shows that a state's failure to meet child-protection expectations is generally not itself a federal constitutional violation.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the controlling federal authority limiting § 1983 liability for a child's death under agency supervision absent state custody.
relevance.PMC-01: It frames why performance monitoring, not constitutional litigation, is the principal check on agency non-performance.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals held that placement on the Responsible Individuals List deprives a person of liberty interests protected by Article I, Section 19 of the North Carolina Constitution, and that the statutory scheme was unconstitutional because it permitted listing without a pre-deprivation hearing at which the director must prove abuse or serious neglect by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: we hold that an individual has a right to notice and an opportunity to be heard before being placed on the RIL

relevance.INP-10: The consequences of escalating a report to an investigative assessment include RIL listing, which now carries pre-deprivation process.
relevance.DEC-01: Where a report is screened out or unsubstantiated, no listing may follow; listing requires a substantiated determination proved at a hearing.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling NC authority on the due-process rights that attach when an agency substantiates abuse or serious neglect and names a responsible individual.
relevance.DEC-06: Choosing a non-court, service-based response avoids the liberty deprivation that triggers these hearing rights.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading NC decision reversing an agency determination for want of constitutionally adequate procedure.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed a neglect adjudication, holding that ICWA did not apply because the mother offered only bare assertions of tribal affiliation and never produced documentation or tribal testimony establishing that the children were Indian children of a federally recognized tribe.
cases.quote: The burden is on the party invoking the Act to show that its provisions are applicable to the case at issue, through documentation or perhaps testimony from a tribe representative.

relevance.INP-11: C.P. states the NC rule on who bears the burden of establishing ICWA applicability and tribal intervention rights in a juvenile case.
relevance.FAIL-05: It defines the evidentiary showing needed before ICWA's placement and cultural-preference protections can be invoked against a placement decision.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals vacated and remanded a juvenile order because the record lacked findings and conclusions establishing subject matter jurisdiction under ICWA, holding that where ICWA gives greater protection to the Indian family than state law, ICWA controls.
cases.quote: where the Act provides a higher standard of protection to the Indian family than is otherwise provided by state law, the ICWA standard prevails

relevance.INP-11: E.G.M. is the NC authority requiring express findings on ICWA applicability and jurisdiction before a court custody proceeding may proceed.
relevance.FAIL-05: Failure to apply ICWA's heightened standards to an Indian child is itself reversible error affecting placement equality.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals reversed a permanency planning order awarding guardianship to non-relatives because the trial court made no findings explaining why placement with the children's paternal grandmother was not in their best interests, as N.C.G.S. § 7B-903(a1) requires, and held that ICWA compliance did not excuse those findings.
cases.quote: Such concerns, however, do not obviate the need for findings of fact under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 7B-903(a1) if the court chooses a nonrelative placement for a juvenile.

relevance.INP-11: The Court treated the move from a voluntary kinship placement to guardianship as a foster care placement subject to ICWA.
relevance.ACT-03: Before a child is placed with non-relatives, the court must first consider and make findings about available relatives.
relevance.ACT-04: E.R. is the leading NC authority enforcing the statutory relative-placement priority at review and permanency planning hearings.
relevance.OUT-03: A guardianship award to non-relatives is reversible without findings rejecting an available relative placement.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed a guardianship award, holding that the proposed guardian's sworn (if unspecific) testimony that she was willing and financially able to care for the child was competent evidence supporting the trial court's verification of adequate resources under N.C.G.S. § 7B-600(c).
cases.quote: our standard of review merely asks if there was competent evidence, even hearsay evidence, at trial to support the trial court's findings

relevance.ACT-04: It sets the evidentiary threshold a kinship caregiver must meet before being appointed guardian.
relevance.OUT-03: N.H. governs the § 7B-600(c) verification that a guardian understands the appointment and has adequate resources.

cases.case_name: Weller v. Department of Social Services
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held that a father stated a procedural due process claim under § 1983 where he alleged that social services transferred custody of his child without any hearing, because a parent is entitled to a state-initiated hearing before deprivation of custody or, in an emergency, promptly afterward.
cases.quote: there is no constitutional requirement of a pre-deprivation hearing under emergency circumstances

relevance.INP-12: Weller sets the Fourth Circuit rule governing protective custody taken without prior judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that an emergency removal must be followed promptly by a hearing that judicially ratifies the agency's action.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the circuit precedent under which a North Carolina parent removed without any hearing states a § 1983 procedural due process claim.

cases.case_name: Jordan ex rel. Jordan v. Jackson
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit upheld an emergency removal statute facially and as applied, holding that a 65-hour delay over a weekend before judicial review did not violate due process where removal was permitted only on imminent danger of death or severe or irremediable injury and judicial review was required within 72 hours.
cases.quote: Due process, however, does not always require prior process.

relevance.INP-12: Jordan is the Fourth Circuit's fullest treatment of the substantive and procedural limits on taking a child into emergency protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: It supplies the imminent-danger standard and the promptness requirement for post-removal judicial review in this circuit.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks the boundary between a lawful exigent removal and one actionable under § 1983 for want of exigency or prompt review.

cases.case_name: Hodge ex rel. Hodge v. Jones
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held that parents cleared of abuse allegations had no clearly established constitutional right to expungement of the agency's investigative records, reversing the denial of qualified immunity because the familial privacy interest in those records is outweighed by legitimate governmental interests in retaining them.
cases.quote: The maxim of familial privacy is neither absolute nor unqualified

relevance.INP-09: It addresses the legitimate governmental interest in retaining investigative records for later oversight and pattern analysis.
relevance.FAIL-03: It shows that record-retention practices criticized as non-compliant are not, without more, federal constitutional violations.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the circuit authority on the constitutional interests at stake when agencies retain or disclose unsubstantiated abuse records.
relevance.PMC-05: It defines the limits of a family's privacy claim against government retention of child-welfare investigative files.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held that a social worker's investigative home visit, entered with the occupant's consent and accompanied by deputies, was not an unreasonable search, and that the officials were entitled to qualified immunity for the entry.
cases.quote: investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context

relevance.INP-12: It governs the Fourth Amendment analysis when caseworkers and law enforcement enter a home together during a child-protection inquiry.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the circuit rule on consent, scope, and reasonableness of caseworker home visits during an investigation.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks when an entry incident to a child-welfare investigation crosses into an actionable Fourth Amendment violation.

cases.case_name: News and Observer Publishing Co. v. Poole
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that SBI investigative reports submitted to a gubernatorial commission became the commission's public records, and that absent a clear statutory exemption all documents meeting the statutory definition of public records must be disclosed for public inspection.
cases.quote: in the absence of clear statutory exemption or exception, documents falling within the definition of "public records" in the Public Records Law must be made available for public inspection

relevance.INP-09: Poole is the principal NC authority supporting public access to the investigative records of state oversight bodies.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the controlling NC case on an agency's refusal to disclose records that fall within Chapter 132.
relevance.PMC-01: Records generated in state performance reviews are presumptively public absent a clear statutory exemption.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and investigative materials held by a state agency are public records unless expressly exempted.
relevance.PMC-03: Materials produced by state-created review bodies are presumptively subject to public inspection.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review materials gathered by or submitted to a state commission are presumptively public records under this rule.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the leading NC transparency decision: exemptions must be clear and statutory, not inferred from policy.
relevance.PMC-06: It supplies the legal baseline for citizen access to the state records on which independent analysis depends.

cases.case_name: Virmani v. Presbyterian Health Services Corp.
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the public's qualified right of access to civil court proceedings and records under Article I, Section 18 was not violated by closing hearings and sealing materials, because the compelling statutory interest in confidential medical peer review outweighed that right and no lesser alternative would protect it.
cases.quote: the compelling countervailing public interest in such high quality public medical care overcomes the qualified public right to open civil court proceedings and records of those proceedings

relevance.FAIL-06: It establishes that North Carolina's access right is qualified and can be overcome only by a compelling, narrowly served interest with no adequate alternative.
relevance.PMC-02: It supplies the framework for testing whether a claimed confidentiality interest justifies withholding audit-related materials.
relevance.PMC-03: It shows the analysis a court applies when a review body asserts statutory confidentiality against public access.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the leading NC authority balancing statutory confidentiality against the constitutional right of access to court records.
relevance.PMC-06: Any transparency demand must be measured against this compelling-interest and least-restrictive-alternative test.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals vacated the visitation portion of a dispositional order because the trial court improperly delegated visitation entirely to the discretion of the custodian instead of establishing an appropriate court-approved visitation plan.
cases.quote: The trial court maintains the responsibility to ensure that an appropriate visitation plan is established within the dispositional order.

relevance.INP-05: Where a family seeks or accepts help short of removal, the court still must fix contact terms rather than leave them to a caregiver's discretion.
relevance.ACT-01: Service and contact arrangements cannot be left to informal discretion once a dispositional order is entered.
relevance.OUT-01: Court-set visitation is the practical engine of reunification and may not be delegated away.
relevance.OUT-03: A guardianship or custody award must still contain a court-established visitation plan for the parent.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals reversed adjudications of neglect and dependency and remanded because the trial court recited allegations rather than making its own findings linking the mother's conduct to the statutory definitions.
cases.quote: The fact that the child has special needs does not automatically render the child dependent or neglected.

relevance.INP-05: A parent's request for help with a child's special needs is not itself a basis for a neglect or dependency finding.
relevance.DEC-01: It confirms that circumstances short of the statutory definitions should not be carried forward as founded findings.
relevance.DEC-03: The agency must prove, and the court must independently find, facts linking parental conduct to the statutory definitions.
relevance.OUT-05: Recited allegations unsupported by independent findings require reversal of the adjudication.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a clean example of appellate reversal of an adjudication for insufficient, non-independent findings.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals upheld the ex parte order directing the mother to cease interfering with the DSS investigation but held that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to award sole temporary custody to the father because no nonsecure custody request had been made and no abuse, neglect, or dependency petition had been filed.
cases.quote: a request for nonsecure custody must be made and a petition must be filed before the court may issue an order for nonsecure custody

relevance.INP-03: The opinion identifies the narrow statutory exception under which a law enforcement officer or DSS worker may take temporary custody without a court order.
relevance.INP-04: It shows the limits on what a court may order during a juvenile investigation absent a filed petition.
relevance.INP-10: It explains the § 7B-303 non-interference mechanism available once an investigation is properly mandated.
relevance.INP-12: It marks the boundary between lawful warrantless temporary custody and a custody order requiring a petition.
relevance.DEC-02: It confirms the court's exclusive original jurisdiction over petitions alleging obstruction of a required investigation.
relevance.DEC-04: Nonsecure custody requires a filed petition and a reasonable factual basis to believe its allegations are true.
relevance.DEC-05: The petition is the jurisdictional precondition to any custodial order in a juvenile case.
relevance.ACT-03: Out-of-home placement by court order cannot precede the filing of a juvenile petition.
relevance.ACT-05: It approves the ex parte non-interference order as a protective tool that does not itself authorize a change of custody.
relevance.FAIL-02: A custody order entered without a petition is void for want of jurisdiction.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held it was plain error to admit an expert's opinion that the child had in fact been sexually abused where there was no supporting physical evidence, while confirming that a properly qualified expert may testify about the characteristics of sexually abused children and whether the alleged victim exhibits them.
cases.quote: However, if a proper foundation has been laid, an expert may testify about the characteristics of sexually abused children and whether an alleged victim exhibits such characteristics.

relevance.INP-07: Towe governs what a medical or clinical evaluation of a child may and may not be offered to prove once a disclosure is reported.
relevance.DEC-03: It limits reliance on expert opinion that abuse occurred when no physical findings support the diagnosis, a recurring basis for substantiation.
relevance.ACT-06: It defines the evidentiary weight of child medical evaluations obtained after an urgent examination.

cases.case_name: Smith v. Jackson County Board of Education
cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed denial of dismissal, holding that a school resource officer's failure to report known child abuse fell outside the conduct the public duty doctrine shields and that the remaining negligence claims came within the special relationship and special duty exceptions.
cases.quote: Hess' failure to report known child abuse was, therefore, outside the scope of conduct generally associated with law enforcement, and the public duty doctrine does not bar this claim.

relevance.INP-01: It is the principal NC decision holding that a mandated reporter's failure to report can support tort liability notwithstanding the public duty doctrine.
relevance.INP-03: It concerns a school resource officer and defines when law enforcement's reporting failure is actionable.
relevance.INP-08: It arises from school personnel who knew of abuse of a student and did not report it.
relevance.OUT-06: It identifies the state-law avenue for redress when a child is seriously harmed after officials failed to report.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines the public duty doctrine and its exceptions, the central defense in NC suits over harm following official inaction.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that an adoption decree purporting to add a second parent without terminating the biological parent's rights was void ab initio because Chapter 48 gave the court no subject matter jurisdiction to enter it, while leaving the separate joint custody order undisturbed.
cases.quote: the General Assembly did not vest our courts with subject matter jurisdiction to create the type of adoption attempted here

relevance.OUT-03: It shows that permanency arrangements outside the statutory adoption scheme are void, which is why guardianship or custody orders, not improvised adoptions, must be used.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that N.C.G.S. § 50B-3 does not authorize a district court to order law enforcement to search a defendant's person, vehicle, or residence under an ex parte domestic violence protective order, and that the resulting warrantless search, lacking probable cause and exigency, was unconstitutional.
cases.quote: The plain language of section 50B-3 does not authorize courts to order law enforcement to search a defendant's person, vehicle, or residence under a DVPO.

relevance.INP-03: It limits what law enforcement may do under a civil protective order encountered during a domestic violence or child-safety call.
relevance.ACT-05: Elder is the controlling NC authority on the outer limits of relief a Chapter 50B protective order may contain.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals held that a respondent parent called as a witness by DSS in an abuse, neglect, and dependency hearing is a compelled rather than voluntary witness, so her Fifth Amendment privilege remained available question by question and was violated when she was required to answer.
cases.quote: When a witness is compelled to testify, however, her right to assert the privilege is preserved until such time as an answer to a particular question would incriminate her.

relevance.DEC-02: It governs a parent's privilege against self-incrimination when the agency compels testimony during a parallel investigation or prosecution.
relevance.DEC-03: Findings supporting a substantiated determination cannot rest on testimony compelled in violation of the parent's Fifth Amendment privilege.

cases.court: Court of Appeals of North Carolina
cases.holding: In a case of first impression the Court of Appeals held that Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act is not a defense to a termination of parental rights proceeding and did not bar termination of the intellectually disabled mother's rights.
cases.quote: we hold that the ADA does not prevent the termination of parental rights in the instant case

relevance.FAIL-05: C.M.S. is the controlling NC authority on disability-discrimination claims raised against child welfare agency action, holding the ADA is not a defense to termination though it may bear on the services owed.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that absent a finding that the parents are unfit or have neglected their child's welfare, the parents' constitutionally protected paramount right to custody, care and control prevails over the competing claim of third parties (here, former prospective adoptive parents), so the trial court could not award them custody and did not err in leaving any visitation to the parents' consent.
cases.quote: absent a finding that parents (i) are unfit or (ii) have neglected the welfare of their children, the constitutionally-protected paramount right of parents to custody, care, and control of their children must prevail

relevance.ACT-04: Petersen is the foundational NC Supreme Court holding that relatives or other third parties cannot be given custody over a parent's objection absent unfitness or neglect, and it is the source on which Adams v. Tessener and David N. v. Jason N. are built.
relevance.ACT-06: It establishes that the parents' paramount right extends to controlling their child's care and associations, so the State may not substitute its own judgment about the child's welfare without a finding of unfitness or neglect.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a natural parent's constitutionally protected paramount interest yields to the statutory best-interest test only where the trier of fact finds, on record evidence, conduct inconsistent with that protected status — which includes but is not limited to unfitness, neglect and abandonment — and remanded for a determination whether the mother's period of voluntary nonparent custody was such conduct.
cases.quote: Unfitness, neglect, and abandonment clearly constitute conduct inconsistent with the protected status parents may enjoy.

relevance.ACT-03: Price is the origin of the 'conduct inconsistent with the parent's constitutionally protected status' route by which a fit parent may lose custody of a child to the State or another caregiver, and it holds that such conduct need not rise to the level warranting termination of parental rights.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed an award of custody to a grandmother, holding that a trial court may apply the best-interest-of-the-child test against a natural parent only after the movant first establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the parent's cumulative conduct was inconsistent with his constitutionally protected status.
cases.quote: the trial court's determination that a parent's conduct is inconsistent with his or her constitutionally protected status must be supported by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-04: Owenby is the cleanest modern NC Supreme Court statement that a comparative best-interests judgment cannot justify displacing a parent; clear and convincing proof of unfitness or inconsistent conduct must come first, which is the standard any emergency removal decision must ultimately satisfy.
relevance.ACT-03: It fixes the burden of proof the agency or third party must carry before a child may be placed outside the parental home over the parent's objection.
relevance.FAIL-02: A removal or custody change resting on less than clear and convincing evidence of unfitness or conduct inconsistent with protected status is constitutionally defective under this rule.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held per curiam that it was error to admit a pediatrician's opinion that the child was in fact sexually assaulted where thorough examination and testing revealed no physical evidence of abuse, though on this record the error did not rise to plain error; a properly founded expert may still testify to the profiles of sexually abused children and whether the complainant has consistent characteristics.
cases.quote: absent physical evidence supporting a diagnosis of sexual abuse, such testimony is an impermissible opinion regarding the victim's credibility

relevance.INP-07: Stancil is the controlling NC rule limiting what a medical or clinical evaluation of a child may be offered to prove after a disclosure, and it is the authority State v. Towe applies.
relevance.DEC-03: It bars an agency or prosecutor from resting a determination that abuse occurred on an expert's unsupported opinion that it did, when no physical findings support the diagnosis.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and held that the trial court had authority under N.C.G.S. § 7B-904(d1)(3) to require the mother to create a budgeting plan, and that her failure to do so supported termination under § 7B-1111(a)(2) because her mismanagement of income worsened the instability and inadequate housing that led to the juveniles' removal.
cases.quote: it was entirely appropriate for the court to have ordered respondent to create a budgeting plan

relevance.ACT-02: D.L.W. is the NC Supreme Court predicate for In re B.O.A.: it holds that a court-ordered case plan requirement is valid, and non-compliance with it consequential, where the requirement addresses a condition that contributed to removal even indirectly.
relevance.OUT-01: It defines what counts as reasonable progress in correcting the conditions that led to removal, the measure by which a return home is assessed.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and held that a permanency planning order ceasing reunification need not recite N.C.G.S. § 7B-507's language verbatim so long as its findings address the substance of the statutory requirements, and that an incomplete cease-reunification order may be cured by the findings in the later termination of parental rights order reviewed together with it.
cases.quote: When reviewing the sufficiency of such orders, an appellate court should consider whether the trial court's findings of fact address the substance of the statutory requirements.

relevance.ACT-02: L.M.T. is the controlling NC Supreme Court authority on the findings a court must make before relieving the agency of court-ordered reunification efforts (former § 7B-507(b), now § 7B-901(c)).
relevance.OUT-01: It governs the point at which reunification ceases to be the plan, and therefore the findings a parent must attack to preserve a return home.
relevance.FAIL-01: It defines when an appellate court may and may not reverse a cease-reunification order for deficient findings, correcting the Court of Appeals' verbatim-recitation rule.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a trial court retains jurisdiction to enter an order terminating parental rights while an appeal of a custody order in the same juvenile case is pending, rejecting the Court of Appeals' contrary rule and explaining that N.C.G.S. § 7B-1003 expands rather than limits trial court jurisdiction in child custody proceedings.
cases.quote: we hold a trial court retains jurisdiction to terminate parental rights during the pendency of a custody order appeal in the same case

relevance.INP-04: R.T.W. maps the jurisdictional architecture of Chapter 7B, identifying which article confers jurisdiction and standing when a juvenile matter is opened and carried forward by court order.
relevance.DEC-05: It explains how jurisdiction over a dependency case, once properly obtained by petition, coexists with the separate jurisdictional grant governing termination proceedings.
relevance.OUT-04: It confirms the trial court's continuing jurisdiction to modify or vacate custody orders in light of changed circumstances or the juvenile's needs, the mechanism by which a case continues toward or past permanency.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court vacated a termination order and remanded for new findings, holding that the trial court's findings of fact were insufficient to support termination on either neglect or willful abandonment, while rejecting the father's separate contention that the trial court's questioning of witnesses showed bias.
cases.quote: the trial court's findings of fact are insufficient to support its determination that respondent-father's parental rights in Nancy were subject to termination on the grounds of neglect and abandonment

relevance.OUT-05: It is recent NC Supreme Court authority that a petition fails and the order must be vacated where the court's findings, as opposed to recitations of testimony, do not establish the alleged grounds.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the current Supreme Court model for appellate reversal of a petitioner's obtained order for want of adequate findings, and it confirms that a trial court's clarifying questions do not by themselves show partiality.

cases.case_name: Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for two social workers on a mother's § 1983 familial-integrity claim arising from the overnight removal of her children in another state, holding that the contours of the familial-integrity right were not clearly established in these circumstances and that the record showed neither the alleged misrepresentations nor an intrusion severe enough to violate the Constitution, so qualified immunity applied.
cases.quote: A state has a legitimate interest in protecting children from neglect and abuse and in investigating situations that may give rise to such neglect and abuse.

relevance.INP-12: Martin is the twenty-first-century Fourth Circuit decision on social workers who arrange a child's removal without fresh judicial authorization, and it frames the state interest against which such protective custody is measured.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that where legal custody already rests with the agency and a hearing is imminent, a brief removal does not violate a clearly established right, marking the practical limits of the emergency removal inquiry.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the modern circuit authority a North Carolina plaintiff must overcome on qualified immunity when alleging that caseworkers procured an unlawful removal.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that Washington's third-party visitation statute, as applied to order grandparent visitation over the objection of a mother never found unfit and without according her determination any special weight, violated her Fourteenth Amendment due process right to make decisions concerning the care, custody and control of her children.
cases.quote: if a fit parent's decision of the kind at issue here becomes subject to judicial review, the court must accord at least some special weight to the parent's own determination

relevance.ACT-04: Troxel is the federal source of the rule Adams v. Tessener applies in North Carolina: a court may not award custody or visitation to grandparents or other third parties simply because it thinks that arrangement better for the child.
relevance.ACT-06: It establishes the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interests, which is the constitutional starting point whenever the State seeks to override a parent's decision about the child's care or treatment.

cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that UNC-Chapel Hill must release as public records the name, violation and sanction of every student found responsible for violating its sexual assault policy, because FERPA permits but does not compel confidentiality and therefore does not preempt the mandate of North Carolina's Public Records Act.
cases.quote: The Act is intended to be liberally construed to ensure that governmental records be open and made available to the public, subject only to a few limited exceptions.

relevance.FAIL-06: It is the most recent NC Supreme Court authority rejecting an agency's refusal to disclose, holding that a federal statute merely permitting confidentiality does not create an exemption from Chapter 132.
relevance.PMC-02: It narrows the room an agency has to withhold audit or investigative material by insisting that any exception be a genuine statutory command, not a discretionary practice.
relevance.PMC-05: It updates Poole and Virmani for the FOIA/transparency node, supplying twenty-first-century authority that exceptions to the Public Records Act are construed narrowly.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the current legal baseline for citizen demands for state records on which independent accountability analysis depends.

notes: Method: every case below was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its full opinion text read. Each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved majority/lead opinion after whitespace and curly-quote normalization. No quote is taken from a syllabus, headnote, dissent, or concurrence. Where a cluster contained both a lead and a separate opinion (In re Stumbo, In re T.R.P., Lassiter, Santosky, DeShaney, Suter), the lead/majority opinion was identified by its CourtListener opinion type and author and only that text was quoted.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the NC node files were reviewed as candidate names only. None were retained: they are keyword-matched recent listings with synthetic citations. Every entry here replaces that noise.

Courts used, in the priority order required: Supreme Court of North Carolina (nc) first; Court of Appeals of North Carolina (ncctapp) where no Supreme Court authority exists on the point; U.S. Supreme Court (scotus) where the node turns on a federal constitutional or statutory standard (Santosky, Lassiter, DeShaney, Suter); and the Fourth Circuit (ca4) for Section 1983 removal, caseworker-search, foster-care-custody and records-retention claims arising in North Carolina's circuit.
All 37 cases are marked Published on CourtListener. No unpublished memorandum decisions were used.

Date caveat for three clusters. CourtListener's date_filed for the clusters cited here differs from the conventional decision date in three instances, and the date_decided field reports CourtListener's value: Lassiter (cluster 110506) is recorded as 1981-08-28 though 452 U.S. 18 was decided June 1, 1981; Weller (cluster 8987813) is recorded as 1990-04-19 and a duplicate cluster of the same F.2d opinion shows 1990-04-24; Wildauer (cluster 9017727) is recorded as 1993-01-12 (the argument/submission date) while the duplicate cluster for 993 F.2d 369 shows 1993-05-05. The reporter citations and years are unaffected.

In re A.X.M. is flagged Published by CourtListener but the cluster carries only the regional reporter citation 824 S.E.2d 924, with no N.C. App. volume and page recorded. It is cited in the form '824 S.E.2d 924 (N.C. Ct. App. 2019)'. A practitioner should confirm the official N.C. App. parallel cite before filing.

In re The McClatchy Co., No. 29A23 (N.C. May 23, 2024), a 2024 Supreme Court of North Carolina decision on access to court records, was located but not retrieved or read in full and is therefore omitted. Counsel researching PMC-05/FAIL-06 should read it; it may refine News and Observer Publishing Co. v. Poole and Virmani.

Genuine coverage gap at OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out). Targeted searches of nc and ncctapp for extended foster care, jurisdiction past age eighteen, and Foster Care 18-21 / NC Reach issues returned no published appellate decision construing N.C.G.S. Sections 7B-910.1 or 108A-48. OUT-04 is therefore served by In re A.P. (which restates that juvenile-court jurisdiction continues until terminated by order or until the juvenile turns eighteen or is emancipated) and by the federal standard in Suter v. Artist M. (Title IV-E/Chafee requirements are enforced administratively, not privately). This node has only two cases and both are supplied for that structural reason.

The PMC family (PMC-01 through PMC-06) and FAIL-03 concern federal oversight, audit, citizen review panels, fatality commissions and transparency. There is no North Carolina appellate case law construing CAPTA citizen review panels, CFSR performance, the Single Audit Act or the Protect Our Kids Act. These nodes are served by the governing federal standard (Suter v. Artist M.; DeShaney) together with North Carolina's own transparency and confidentiality law (News and Observer Publishing Co. v. Poole; Virmani; Hodge ex rel. Hodge v. Jones). That is a deliberate mapping of the applicable law, not padding.

Practice point on DEC-03. In re W.B.M. held North Carolina's Responsible Individuals List statutes unconstitutional for want of a pre-deprivation hearing; the General Assembly responded by amending Article 3A of Chapter 7B. Counsel must check the current text of N.C.G.S. Sections 7B-320 and 7B-323 before relying on the procedural detail in W.B.M., although its constitutional holding on notice and an opportunity to be heard remains the governing rule.

Practice point on DEC-01/DEC-02. In re Stumbo was decided under the pre-2015 'investigation' terminology of N.C.G.S. Section 7B-302; the statute now speaks of an 'assessment.' The holding that a report must actually allege facts within the Section 7B-101 definitions before the mandatory response and the Section 7B-303 interference remedy are triggered is unaffected by the renaming.

Practice point on ICWA. In re C.P., In re A.R. and In re E.G.M. all predate the 2016 federal ICWA regulations (25 C.F.R. Part 23) and the 2024 federal guidelines; the 'reason to know' inquiry and notice mechanics are now governed more specifically by regulation than these opinions reflect. Haaland v. Brackeen (2023) upheld ICWA against constitutional challenge and was not retrieved in this session. Counsel should read the current regulations alongside these cases.

Practice point on Section 1983. Weller, Jordan, Hodge and Wildauer are all early-1990s Fourth Circuit decisions and remain the circuit's leading authority on emergency removal procedure, caseworker home entry, and retention of unsubstantiated abuse records. They are frequently distinguished on qualified-immunity grounds in later unpublished dispositions; a litigant should shepardize before relying on any of them for a clearly-established-right argument.

Parallel and duplicate clusters. CourtListener holds duplicate clusters for several of these opinions (for example In re T.R.P. at clusters 6833535 and 1284312; Weller at 8987813 and 540031; Wildauer at 9017727 and 606677; In re W.B.M. at 1405237 and 8911880). The cluster_id given is the one whose opinion text was actually retrieved and quoted, chosen for having the fuller reporter citations.

Missing (for a later pass): Petersen v. Rogers, 337 N.C. 397, 445 S.E.2d 901 (1994) — the foundational NC Supreme Court statement of a natural parent's paramount constitutional right to custody and control against third parties. Adams v. Tessener and David N. v. Jason N., relied on heavily at ACT-03, ACT-04, ACT-06 and DEC-04, are built directly on it; citing the derivatives without the source leaves the constitutional chain incomplete.

Missing (for a later pass): Price v. Howard, 346 N.C. 68, 484 S.E.2d 528 (1997) — the origin of the 'conduct inconsistent with the parent's constitutionally protected status' route by which a fit parent may lose custody. Adams expressly reads Petersen and Price together and David N. applies Price's framework; it is the missing half of the two-route rule the brief relies on at ACT-03 and ACT-04.

Missing (for a later pass): Owenby v. Young, 356 N.C. 615, 575 S.E.2d 26 (2002) — NC Supreme Court confirmation that a determination of conduct inconsistent with protected status must rest on clear and convincing evidence and that a comparative best-interests judgment is not enough. It is the cleanest modern statement of the standard the brief attributes to Adams at DEC-04, ACT-03 and FAIL-02.

Missing (for a later pass): State v. Stancil, 355 N.C. 266, 559 S.E.2d 788 (2002) — the controlling NC rule that an expert may not testify that sexual abuse in fact occurred absent physical evidence, because such testimony is an impermissible opinion on the victim's credibility. Towe is an application of Stancil and quotes it for the very proposition the brief cites Towe for at INP-07 and DEC-03.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.L.W., 368 N.C. 835, 788 S.E.2d 162 (2016) — NC Supreme Court authority on the 7B-1111(a)(2) willfulness and reasonable-progress ground and on case plan provisions whose connection to the removal conditions is indirect. B.O.A. reasons expressly from D.L.W.; it is the predicate authority for ACT-02 and OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re L.M.T., 367 N.C. 165, 752 S.E.2d 453 (2013) — NC Supreme Court decision on the findings a trial court must make before relieving an agency of reunification efforts (former 7B-507(b), now 7B-901(c)). ACT-02 and OUT-01 currently rest on the Court of Appeals' L.G.I. for cessation-of-reunification law where controlling Supreme Court authority exists.

Missing (for a later pass): In re R.T.W., 359 N.C. 539, 614 S.E.2d 489 (2005) — NC Supreme Court authority on juvenile-court jurisdiction and the continuing effect of dispositional orders in abuse, neglect and dependency cases. It is cited inside T.R.P. itself and is directly responsive to the jurisdictional questions the brief loads onto INP-04, DEC-05 and OUT-04.

Missing (for a later pass): In re N.D.A., 373 N.C. 71, 833 S.E.2d 768 (2019) — current NC Supreme Court authority on the 7B-600(c) verification that a proposed guardian understands the appointment and has adequate resources. ACT-04 and OUT-03 presently rest on In re N.H., a divided Court of Appeals panel, where controlling and more recent Supreme Court law is available.

Missing (for a later pass): Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services, 346 F.3d 502 (4th Cir. 2003) — the modern Fourth Circuit decision on a social worker's removal of children without a court order and the qualified immunity analysis that follows. The brief concedes that Weller, Jordan, Wildauer and Hodge are all early-1990s decisions; Martin is the twenty-first-century circuit authority expected at INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the controlling federal statement of the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interests and that a court may not override parental decision-making merely to reach a better result. Adams quotes it for exactly the proposition the brief cites Adams for at ACT-06 and DEC-04; the federal source belongs in the brief in its own right.

Missing (for a later pass): DTH Media Corp. v. Folt, 374 N.C. 292, 841 S.E.2d 251 (2020) — the most recent NC Supreme Court public-records decision, narrowly construing a claimed statutory exemption and ordering disclosure. FAIL-06, PMC-02 and PMC-05 currently rest on Poole (1992) and Virmani (1999) with no authority from the last twenty-five years.

=== ADDITIONS, 2026-09-20 PASS (gap closure). The eleven 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes above are retained verbatim as the record of what the verifier flagged; ten of the eleven authorities have now been retrieved from CourtListener, read in full, and added below. The pre-existing notes are not edits of the brief's history.

Added Petersen v. Rogers, 337 N.C. 397, 445 S.E.2d 901 (1994) (cluster 1310933) for ACT-04, ACT-06: it is the foundational NC Supreme Court holding that, absent a finding of unfitness or neglect of the children's welfare, the parents' paramount constitutional right to custody, care and control defeats a third party's custody claim — the source on which Adams v. Tessener, Price v. Howard and David N. v. Jason N. all build. The verifier also sought Petersen at ACT-03 and DEC-04; both nodes were already at the six-case ceiling once Price and Owenby were mapped there, so Petersen is carried at ACT-04 (its own facts: third parties seeking custody) and ACT-06 (parental control over the child's care and associations).

Added Price v. Howard, 346 N.C. 68, 484 S.E.2d 528 (1997) (cluster 1232602) for ACT-03: it originates the 'conduct inconsistent with the parent's constitutionally protected status' route by which a fit parent may lose custody, holds that such conduct need not rise to the statutory level warranting termination, and supplies the missing half of the two-route rule the brief previously drew only from Adams and David N.

Added Owenby v. Young (cluster 1305485) for DEC-04, ACT-03, FAIL-02: it is the clearest NC Supreme Court statement that the best-interest test may be applied against a natural parent only after clear and convincing proof of conduct inconsistent with protected status, which is the standard an emergency removal decision must ultimately satisfy and the standard a Section 1983 unlawful-removal claim invokes.

Citation correction for Owenby v. Young. The verifier cited '356 N.C. 615, 575 S.E.2d 26 (2002)'. The CourtListener cluster actually retrieved and read in this session (1305485) carries the official citations 357 N.C. 142 and 579 S.E.2d 264 with a date_filed of 2003-05-02, and the opinion text is the Martin, J. merits opinion reversing the Court of Appeals. The 2002 reference is most likely the order allowing discretionary review. The entry uses the retrieved citation; counsel should cite 357 N.C. 142, 579 S.E.2d 264 (2003).

Added State v. Stancil, 355 N.C. 266, 559 S.E.2d 788 (2002) (cluster 1337407) for INP-07, DEC-03: it is the controlling NC rule — applied, not created, by State v. Towe — that absent physical evidence an expert may not opine that sexual abuse in fact occurred, because that is an impermissible opinion on the child's credibility. The opinion is a short per curiam of the full Court; the quote is from that per curiam, and the Court modified and affirmed after finding the error did not rise to plain error on the record.

Added In re D.L.W., 368 N.C. 835, 788 S.E.2d 162 (2016) (cluster 3212121, opinion 3212015) for ACT-02, OUT-01: it is the NC Supreme Court predicate for In re B.O.A. on the trial court's authority under Section 7B-904(d1)(3) to impose case plan requirements addressing conditions that contributed to removal, and on non-compliance as a Section 7B-1111(a)(2) ground. It was not added to OUT-02, which was already at the six-case ceiling.

Added In re L.M.T., 367 N.C. 165, 752 S.E.2d 453 (2013) (cluster 2677889, lead opinion 9799880 by Newby, J.) for ACT-02, OUT-01, FAIL-01: it is the controlling Supreme Court authority on the findings required before an agency is relieved of reunification efforts, holding that the findings must address the substance rather than the verbatim words of the statute and that a deficient cease-reunification order may be cured by the termination order reviewed with it. The cluster also contains a separate concurrence (opinion 9799881), which was not quoted.

Added In re R.T.W., 359 N.C. 539, 614 S.E.2d 489 (2005) (cluster 6832153, lead opinion 6719257) for INP-04, DEC-05, OUT-04: it is the Supreme Court authority, cited inside In re T.R.P., on juvenile-court jurisdiction and the continuing effect of custody and dispositional orders, holding that a pending custody appeal does not divest the trial court of jurisdiction to terminate parental rights.

Added In re N.D.A. (cluster 4675180, opinion 4452433) for OUT-05, FAIL-01 — NOT for the point the verifier described. The verifier characterized In re N.D.A., 373 N.C. 71, 833 S.E.2d 768 (2019), as NC Supreme Court authority on the Section 7B-600(c) verification that a proposed guardian understands the appointment and has adequate resources. The opinion actually retrieved and read (Ervin, J., filed 1 November 2019, No. 184A19) is a termination of parental rights appeal on the grounds of neglect and willful abandonment; it says nothing about guardianship verification. The case is real, published and on point for insufficiency of findings, so it is mapped where it genuinely belongs. The verifier's description of its subject matter is not confirmed.

Could not verify: NC Supreme Court authority on the Section 7B-600(c) guardianship verification requirement. Targeted searches of the nc court for the statutory language ('guardian understands the legal significance of the appointment', 'adequate resources', Section 7B-600) returned no on-point Supreme Court decision; In re J.A.J., 2022-NCSC-85, was retrieved and read and is a termination case, not a verification case. ACT-04 and OUT-03 therefore continue to rest in part on the Court of Appeals' In re N.H., 255 N.C. App. 501, which remains the best published authority located on that point.

Added Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services, 346 F.3d 502 (4th Cir. 2003) (cluster 2967846, lead opinion 9813269 by Widener, J.) for INP-12, DEC-04, FAIL-02: it is the modern Fourth Circuit treatment of social workers who procure a child's removal without fresh judicial authorization and of the qualified immunity that follows, updating the early-1990s Weller/Jordan/Wildauer/Hodge line the brief previously relied on alone. Judge Traxler's dissent (opinion 9813270) was not quoted.

Added Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) (cluster 1087668, lead opinion 9526957) for ACT-04, ACT-06: it is the federal source of the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interests and of the rule that a court must give a fit parent's own determination special weight — the proposition Adams v. Tessener quotes and the brief previously cited only through Adams. Justice O'Connor's opinion is a four-Justice plurality announcing the judgment of the Court, not a majority opinion; the quote is taken from that controlling lead opinion, and the two dissents in the cluster (opinions 9526960 and 9526962) were not used. Counsel should cite it as a plurality. It was not added to DEC-04, which was already at the six-case ceiling.

Added DTH Media Corp. v. Folt (cluster 4750577, opinion 4530924) for FAIL-06, PMC-02, PMC-05, PMC-06: it is the most recent NC Supreme Court public-records decision, holding that FERPA merely permits and does not compel confidentiality and so does not displace the Public Records Act's disclosure mandate. It gives the transparency nodes authority from the last five years rather than only Poole (1992) and Virmani (1999). The CourtListener cluster carries no reporter citation, so the entry uses slip form, No. 142PA18 (N.C. May 1, 2020); the verifier's reported official cite, 374 N.C. 292, 841 S.E.2d 251, could not be confirmed from the cluster record and should be checked before filing. The retrieved document is a combined opinion containing Justice Davis's dissent (joined by Justices Ervin and Earls); the quote was taken only from the Opinion of the Court, before the dissent begins.

Under-populated nodes closed without new retrieval. Four nodes carried only one case before this pass: INP-04, DEC-06, ACT-02 and ACT-06. In each instance the fix was to extend node_map to cases already in this brief whose relevance objects already addressed the node but which had been omitted from the map during reconciliation — In re A.P. at INP-04; Dobson v. Harris and In re W.B.M. at DEC-06; In re Ballard at ACT-02; In re Stumbo and State v. Towe at ACT-06 — together with the new additions above. No case was added to a node its opinion does not actually support.

DEC-06 (Differential Response / Alternative Response) remains the thinnest node in the brief. Searches of nc and ncctapp located no published North Carolina appellate decision construing the family assessment response track of N.C.G.S. Section 7B-302(a) or the differential response system as such. The node is served by Stumbo (a low-level report may be answered informally without invoking Chapter 7B), Dobson (reporter immunity permits non-court triage), and W.B.M. (a non-court, service-based response avoids the liberty deprivation that triggers hearing rights). That is the applicable law, not an evasion.

ACT-06 (Emergency Medical/Psychological Care) has no North Carolina appellate decision squarely authorizing or reviewing court-ordered emergency medical or psychological treatment of a child over parental objection; a targeted nc search returned only criminal cases. The node is therefore served by the constitutional framework (Troxel; Petersen; Adams), by Stumbo on the proportionality of intrusion, and by Towe on the evidentiary use of a post-examination child medical evaluation.

Quote-length note. The Petersen v. Rogers quote runs to thirty-three words, slightly over the thirty-word norm used throughout this brief. It was kept at full length because the rule's two express exceptions — unfitness and neglect of the children's welfare — are the operative qualifications; any shorter exact substring would state the parental right as absolute and materially misdescribe the holding. No ellipsis was used and the text is an exact substring of the opinion.

Case count. This brief now carries forty-four distinct cases, above the twenty-to-forty working range, because the gap-closure pass required adding every named leading authority that could be verified. Every added case is mapped to at least one node and no node exceeds six cases. Nodes at the six-case ceiling after this pass, and therefore closed to further additions without a re-balance, are DEC-03, DEC-04, ACT-03, ACT-04, OUT-02, FAIL-01 and FAIL-02.

Missing (for a later pass): Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) — the foundational federal holding that an unwed father is entitled to a hearing on fitness before his children are taken; Petersen v. Rogers expressly builds on it and the brief's entire ACT-03/ACT-04/DEC-04 constitutional chain rests on it without citing it.

Missing (for a later pass): Prince v. Massachusetts, 321 U.S. 158 (1944) — the controlling statement of the State's parens patriae power over a child's welfare and its limits against parental authority; it is the classic authority for ACT-06 (emergency medical/psychological care over parental objection), which the brief concedes is unserved.

Missing (for a later pass): Wyman v. James, 400 U.S. 309 (1971) — the Supreme Court's holding that a caseworker's home visit is not a Fourth Amendment search in the criminal sense; Wildauer applies exactly this reasoning, and DEC-02/INP-12 cite the circuit derivative without the federal source.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — upheld ICWA against Article I, anticommandeering and equal protection challenges; the brief's own notes flag it as unretrieved, and INP-11/FAIL-05 currently rest on NC opinions that all predate the 2016 ICWA regulations.

Missing (for a later pass): Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989) — the Supreme Court's foundational ICWA decision on domicile and exclusive tribal jurisdiction; INP-11 turns on jurisdiction and has no federal ICWA authority at all.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) — limits ICWA sections 1912(d) and (f) where the parent never had custody; it is the authority most often dispositive in a contested state-court ICWA placement, and is absent from INP-11 and FAIL-05.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Helms, 127 N.C. App. 505, 491 S.E.2d 672 (1997) — the NC rule that a neglect adjudication requires some physical, mental or emotional impairment, or a substantial risk of it, as a consequence of the parent's conduct; DEC-03 currently rests on Montgomery (1984) without the impairment requirement that NC courts actually apply.

Missing (for a later pass): Braswell v.
